collection.credit:
* V9 "Age of Terrible Ideas": event prose, material applications,
  trial and consequence branches by ChatGPT. Core requests for intense
  conflict, fights, false guilt, courts, imprisonment, reconciliation,
  and the sixteen specific bizarre materials by Lorsieab2.

ledger.why: designer note: custody only if the patch supports it (it does not), so the source's default, supervised restitution, is shown

items.text: The culprit admits envy and apologizes sincerely.
The culprit insists the artwork deserved it. The community condemns the act without demanding instant forgiveness.
The victim refuses to reconcile. The culprit must accept that.

intro.name: The exhibition
intro.text: A joint Isolan-village art exhibition ends in disaster. A display of polished pearls is found shattered, and glittering gemstone powder has been scattered across a prized carved panel.

question.name: Accusations
question.text: An Isolan artist accuses a village Master Builder. The builder accuses an Isolan rival. A frightened apprentice confesses before anyone asks a question. The neutral arbiter calls for order.

choices.label: Convene a public hearing with neutral rules.
Pause the exhibition and preserve the damaged work.

e1.text: A fallen shelf caused the damage. Neither rival is guilty.

e2.text: One rival deliberately struck the display.

e3.text: The apprentice knocked it over by accident and panicked.

e4.text: The powder came from an unrelated art project.

c1.text: The apprentice was afraid the mentor would be punished.

c2.text: The apprentice thought a confession would end the fighting.

c3.text: The apprentice actually caused the damage by accident.

c4.text: The apprentice saw the real culprit and is afraid to name (culprit.him/her).

m1.text: The rivals are bitter enemies but neither damaged the display.

m2.text: One rival wanted to win so badly that (rival.he/she) sabotaged it.

m3.text: One rival made a cruel joke, not the physical damage. The joke is addressed separately.

m4.text: The rivals were secretly collaborating on a surprise exhibit; their secrecy caused a misunderstanding.

h1.text: The arbiter catches a witness inventing details to protect a friend.

h2.text: The accused screams, 'YOU HAVE HATED ME SINCE THE DAY WE MET!' The rival replies, 'YES, BUT THAT DOESN'T MAKE YOU GUILTY!'

h3.text: A witness admits to tampering and offers restitution.

h4.text: The arbiter refuses to treat the apprentice's fear as proof.

p1.text: The pearls are recoverable and the panel can be repaired.

p2.text: The artwork is permanently damaged; its maker grieves the loss.

p3.text: A child finds a missing pearl inside a decorative coconut.

p4.text: A visiting artisan offers a restoration method.

exoneration.name: Exoneration
exoneration.text: The arbiter publicly clears those against whom there is no evidence. The rivals may apologize, remain hostile, or begin to trust each other. The apprentice learns that confessing to a thing one didn't do can make the truth harder to find.

intentional.name: Intentional damage
intentional.text:
The culprit is identified by evidence, not rumor. The arbiter orders restitution, a public correction and proportionate consequences.
{DAMAGE}

accident.name: Accident
accident.text: The apprentice admits the accident. The adults realize their furious accusations frightened a young person into hiding the truth. They apologize; the apprentice helps repair what can be repaired.

bittersweet.name: Bittersweet
bittersweet.text: The damaged art cannot be made exactly as it was. The artist may restore it imperfectly, create a new work, or leave it unfinished. A former rival says, 'I hated that piece. I never wanted it destroyed.' The artist replies, 'I wish you had said that yesterday.'
